reasoning: Urban Palestinian turns ث into t, so ثنتين is said tinteen, with the dual ending -een. This is the feminine form used in counting and with feminine nouns; the masculine is itneen.

Literally 'may you bury me', meaning 'I hope to die before you'. The English gives the affectionate sense. This is the masculine form, and ق is a glottal stop in this everyday verb. The prefix vowel (ti- or ta-) varies, so I am only medium confident.
ذ becomes z in iza, as in Palestinian 'if'. The phrase is common across the Levant and has no distinctly Palestinian replacement.
Uses shu and the b- present prefix, both markers of Palestinian speech. Word-initial hamza in abuuk is only a vowel seat, so nothing is written for it.
ص is emphatic, so a capital S. على plus ـي becomes 3alayy with a doubled y. Literally 'small on me', which is the idiom for 'too small for me'.
Taa marbuta after م is e. ص is emphatic (S). Used for fingerprints and for fingerprint attendance systems.

Urban Palestinian does not keep the interdental ظ. It is realised as an emphatic stop, written D, and doubled by the shadda. I respelled with ض so the TTS voice says it that way. Common everyday word.
ض is emphatic (D). Taa marbuta after ل is e. The word is standard across the Levant.
Form V participle of the loan-derived verb نرفز, meaning on edge or irritated. Common in Palestinian and the rest of the Levant.
An abstract word of MSA origin that Palestinians do use when talking about morals and society, so it keeps [q]. It is the plural of قيمة.
Form II verb yisallim with the -ak suffix for a male addressee. A common Palestinian reply to thanks or a good wish.
The shadda doubles y, and the ending is e after y. Palestinians say 3amaliyye alone for a surgical operation; it also means a military operation.
ق is a glottal stop, the shadda doubles d, and taa marbuta after ح is e. Understood across the Levant, but in Ramallah ولّاعة (wallaa3a) is at least as common.
ما negates the past with kaan, and ti7ki is the you (m.) present. ض is emphatic (D) in mafruuD.
ث becomes t in taanye, so I respelled with ت. The ending is a after ر in marra and e after ي in taanye. It means 'again' or 'another time'.
Form VI past, he-form: he reconciled or made up (with someone, used with ma3). ص is emphatic (S) and ح is 7.

The dialect rules list ايش as not the Ramallah 'what'. It belongs to other regional speech (Gulf, Hijaz, parts of Syria and Jordan), and Ramallah speakers say shu. Flagged as a variant, not as an error in the English.
The colloquial hundreds are compounds (khamsmiyye, not MSA khamsumi'a). Taa marbuta after ي is e. A helping vowel (khamsimiyye) is also heard.
Standard colloquial mil7 with ح written 7. Everyday word.

The colloquial form is 'issiis, with ق as a glottal stop and the shadda doubling s. Palestinian Christians also say خوري (khoori) for a priest, and the MSA form is qissiis. Vowels are the least certain part.
Uses the b- present prefix with shu and illi, all Palestinian markers. ص is emphatic (S) in Saar.
خشم is associated with Gulf, Iraqi and Bedouin speech and is not the usual urban Ramallah word, which is anf (or manKhar). I can't call it Lebanese or Syrian either, so I marked it unsure.
il- stays il- before ي, which is a moon letter. yoom has a long oo, and the shadda doubles r in 7arr.
A Palestinian proverb: ق in قد is a glottal stop and is doubled before the possessive. ijreek is the dual of ijr 'leg', with 'your'. A variant replaces li7aaf with fraash.
The hamza after the prefix and article is medial, so it is written '. ba3deen means 'then' or 'afterwards' with long ee. The ellipses are not romanized.
